title: Genevieve (3 January)
hook: a young woman who calmed Paris during the siege of Attila

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was litany, and your line was pray for us: a church full of names. Today we start walking the calendar, saint by saint, in January. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

Rumors arrive before armies do. In the story, word reaches Paris that Attila and his Huns are coming, burning cities on the way. People start loading carts. Valuables wrapped in blankets, children on top, the city gates jammed. Neighbors shout advice across the street. Leaving seems like the only sane thing to do. And one young woman stands in the middle of the panic and says: stay. Don't run. Pray. Her name is today's word.
screen: `RUMORS ARRIVE BEFORE ARMIES.` → `CARTS AT THE CITY GATES.` → `ONE VOICE: STAY. PRAY.`

segments.voice: Genevieve lived in Paris in the days when Roman Gaul was coming apart. An early account of her life tells her story, and the Church remembers her in early January. She was a consecrated virgin: not a nun in a convent, but a woman who had given her life to God and lived it out in the city, praying, fasting and caring for people. When the news of Attila came, the account says, she gathered the women of Paris to pray, and she begged the men not to carry their goods away. The cities they fled to, she warned, would not be safe; Paris would be protected. That did not go down well. Some citizens called her a false prophet, and, the account says, they talked about stoning her or throwing her in the river. Then a churchman arrived from Auxerre, where the bishop Germanus had once praised her, and he spoke up for her, and the crowd backed off. And Attila's army turned away. It never reached Paris. Catholics honor Genevieve as the patron of Paris, and her story sits easily next to a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." What she did is ordinary and very hard. She didn't fight. She didn't flee. In a crowd that was spinning, she stayed still, prayed, and asked others to do the same. Calm can be contagious. So can panic. She chose which one to pass on.
screen: `A CONSECRATED WOMAN IN THE CITY.` · `STAY AND PRAY, WHEN EVERYONE RUNS.` · `THE CROWD TURNS ON HER.` · `THE ARMY TURNS AWAY.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD KEEP THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your city in a crisis. Settle into the sit and bring your own town to mind. Not the whole map: one street, one hospital, one bus stop. Think of whatever it's facing right now, a storm, a shortage, a fear, a loss. Breathe slowly, the way Genevieve stood still. If you pray, you can ask God to keep your city, or ask Saint Genevieve to pray for it. If you don't, simply hold your city in mind, calmly, without fixing anything. The bell holds the time.
Genevieve. A young woman of Paris who, in the story, urged the city to stay and pray when Attila's army came. Patron of Paris, remembered in early January.
Your line: she calmed the city. Today, when a group chat, a meeting or a kitchen starts to spin, be the slowest, calmest voice in the room once. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Genevieve's memory in early January, especially in Paris, where she is honored as the city's patron and people pray for the city in her name.

what it means: a consecrated young woman who calmed a panicking city by praying and asking it to stay.
what a scholar hears: the story comes from an early account of her life, which also records the crowd turning on her and a churchman from Auxerre defending her.
